analysis.one_liner: Sets staggered 18-year terms for Supreme Court justices with a new appointment every two years.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote since its introduction, and it has no Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how Supreme Court justices are chosen. Instead of lifetime appointments, a new justice would join the Court every two years to serve an 18-year term, so every president gets two appointments per term no matter when vacancies happen. Justices who complete 18 years would move to a part-time 'Senior Justice' status and could fill in when a seat is temporarily empty. It would also force the Senate's hand: if the Senate doesn't vote on a nominee within 120 days, the nominee is seated anyway. Justices already on the Court when the bill passes keep their lifetime seats and are not touched by the new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans gain a Court whose membership turns over on a predictable schedule, so no single generation of justices locks in control for decades, and a president's appointments can't be blocked indefinitely by a Senate majority that simply never schedules a vote.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting regular Supreme Court turnover

how_it_helps.text: The President would nominate one justice every two years, in the first and third years after each presidential election, creating a fixed, predictable rotation instead of the current system where timing depends on when a justice dies or retires.

After 18 years a justice would be 'deemed retired from regular active service' and become a Senior Justice, who can handle cases only when assigned by the Chief Justice — a soft term limit rather than removal from the bench.

If the Senate takes no action on a nominee within 120 days, the Senate is deemed to have waived its advice-and-consent role and the nominee is seated, closing the loophole where a majority can kill a nomination by refusing to schedule a vote.
When a seat opens unexpectedly, the most recent Senior Justice would be assigned to fill it until a new appointment is made, so the Court keeps a full bench during vacancies.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting senators lose part of their power to block Supreme Court nominees by stalling, and the political party that currently holds a favorable Court composition gives up the ability to preserve it through long-lived justices — though under this bill's text, current justices are exempt, so no existing member's seat is affected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Senate majorities and incumbent justices' lifetime tenure

drawbacks.text: Most seriously, the bill attempts to change life tenure by ordinary statute, but the Constitution gives justices life tenure during 'good Behaviour' and critics across the legal spectrum argue Congress cannot shorten it without a constitutional amendment, so the 18-year limit could be challenged as unconstitutional the moment it took effect.

The 120-day automatic-seating rule conflicts with the Constitution's requirement that appointments be made 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate', and critics argue Congress cannot waive a Senate power the Constitution grants directly.

The bill grandfathers every current justice: none is counted toward the new nine-junior panel and none is required to retire, so the Court's present composition — and its current ideological balance — would be unchanged for years or decades until natural retirements happen.
The new panel rule — the nine most junior justices hear cases — could push established, senior justices off major cases in their final years, a mechanical change with no direct precedent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Regular, staggered appointments would make the Court's makeup less dependent on the luck of timing and would end both vacancy-holding and lifetime tenures stretching 30-plus years — a real gain for the public over the long run. But the bill's central device is on shaky constitutional ground, and by exempting all current justices it does nothing about the Court as it exists today; its benefits would only accumulate generations of appointments from now. An honest supporter would acknowledge this is a long-term reform with a real legal-risk asterisk, not an immediate fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since February 2025, with the Congress still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Supreme Court Term Limits and Regular Appointments Act of 2025 on February 6, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — no further action appears in its history.
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows no Republicans.

Under the bill, appointments to the Court would occur every two years, justices would serve 18-year terms before becoming Senior Justices, and the Senate would have 120 days to act on a nominee or the nominee is seated without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo wins: sitting justices keep lifetime tenure with no turnover schedule, and Senate majorities keep the ability to stall or kill Supreme Court nominees by never scheduling a vote. The bill's backers gained nothing beyond a referral to committee.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing 18-year staggered Supreme Court terms and a 120-day Senate deadline on nominees.

for.name: 8 of 217 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Beyer, Tlaib, Casten, Omar, Goldman, Vargas, Lee, Ansari)

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action on the bill after it was referred on February 6, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters are Democrats (the sponsor plus 8 cosponsors of 217 House Democrats); no Republican cosponsored the bill, and a Republican-controlled House committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill exempts every justice appointed before enactment from the 18-year limit and from the new rotation panel, so current justices keep lifetime tenure indefinitely. The public gets a term-limit system that does not apply to the Court as it is actually staffed today.

industries.industry: Senate majorities (whichever party holds the majority)
industries.note: The 120-day waiver strips a Senate majority of its most effective tool for blocking a president's Court nominees — simply never holding a vote. Ordinary presidents and nominees gain; incumbent Senate control over the bench shrinks.

industries.industry: Presidents and national party organizations invested in Court control
industries.note: Every president would get two Court appointments per term on a fixed schedule, ending the lottery of vacancies, but also ending the possibility of stacking a durable ideological majority for decades. Over time this lowers the stakes of each appointment for the parties and raises predictability for the public.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing, no markup, no Republican cosponsors, and a divided Congress, a bill like this almost always dies quietly in committee at the end of the session. Its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress; a constitutional amendment route is the only version courts are likely to uphold, and that path is far harder to enact.
